:::{#exm-outer-product-transpose}
#### Transposing an outer product

For $\vecf{u} = (1, 2, 3)$ and $\vecf{v} = (4, 5)$,
[the example of an outer product](#exm-outer-product) found the $3 \times 2$ [matrix](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix) $\oprod{\vecf{u}}{\vecf{v}}$.
Swapping the two vectors gives its [transpose](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-transpose):

$$
\ba
\oprod{\vecf{v}}{\vecf{u}}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of the outer product)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
4 \cd 1 & 4 \cd 2 & 4 \cd 3 \\
5 \cd 1 & 5 \cd 2 & 5 \cd 3
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(entry } (i, j) \text{ is } v_i u_j \text{)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix}
4 & 8 & 12 \\
5 & 10 & 15
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\ea
$$

Each [row](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-row) of this matrix is a [column](linear-algebra.qmd#def-matrix-column) of $\oprod{\vecf{u}}{\vecf{v}}$,
as @thm-outer-product-transpose says.

<!-- no-figure: the example multiplies out one small matrix -->

:::
